programmes.historicalNote: The first successful Molniya communications satellite flew in 1965. Twelve-hour elliptical orbits offer a distinct alternative to geostationary coverage.

options.label: Global precision constellation

programmes.name: Satellite Navigation & Precision Timing

programmes.historicalNote: US Transit was operational in 1964 in low polar orbit. This catalogue entry is a new precision-timing/MEO architecture; Transit heritage does not provide a completed modern navigation constellation.

options.label: Recoverable imaging satellites

options.label: Secure electronic imaging relay

options.label: Frequent-revisit constellation
options.detail: Study more spacecraft and launches to reduce coverage gaps. Additional satellites require manufacture, ground processing and continuing replacement.

programmes.name: Strategic Orbital Reconnaissance Network
programmes.description: Integrate precision pointing, secure mission control, image recovery or relay and a continuing interpretation service. Coverage has revisit gaps and replacement costs.
programmes.historicalNote: Both powers operated reconnaissance spacecraft by 1970. This represents an expensive follow-on system rather than universal real-time visibility.

options.label: Earth-orbit transfer demonstration

programmes.name: Orbital Propellant Depot Demonstrator

programmes.historicalNote: NASA contractor studies considered Earth- and lunar-orbit depots in 1971. The study did not create a flight-qualified or funded operational depot.

options.label: Teleoperated traverse

options.label: Polar science package

options.label: Long-duration survival tests

options.label: Deeper drilling package

options.label: Landing-site science campaign
options.detail: Study orbital survey and surface instrument support for choosing scientifically valuable sites. Survey support is helpful rather than a universal mandatory route.

programmes.name: Robotic Lunar Sample Return
programmes.description: Develop landing, drilling, surface ascent, Earth-return guidance and a recoverable sample capsule. Each stage may leave a scientifically useful partial success without returning material.
programmes.historicalNote: Luna 16 returned samples in September 1970, after earlier failures. Sample return is a demanding independent robotic branch.

programmes.historicalNote: Mars 3 made brief surface contact in 1971; Viking launched in 1975 and landed in 1976. A completed descent is not automatically a long-lived scientific success.

outcomeDetails.full_success: Controlled Mars landing confirmed; the surface laboratory completes its accepted scientific campaign. Sustained Mars surface science is qualified.
outcomeDetails.partial_success: Surface contact or brief telemetry received, but the accepted science campaign is incomplete. Sustained Mars surface science remains unqualified.
outcomeDetails.objective_failure: Entry, descent, landing or surface activation failed. No accepted Mars surface science capability; corrective engineering and review are required.
outcomeDetails.catastrophic_failure: The lander is lost during arrival or activation. An extended technical investigation is required before another attempt.

programmes.historicalNote: NERVA achieved ground tests and was cancelled in 1973 before flight. Completing a flight demonstrator is an alternate history programme with additional cost, political exposure and technical risk.

options.detail: Prioritise a large optical payload, human target selection and secure intelligence processing. Crew exposure and replacement launches remain significant.

options.detail: Study a film-return architecture with separate recovery procedures. Recovery failure can erase the value of otherwise successful imaging.

options.label: Civil conversion study

programmes.name: Almaz Crewed Reconnaissance Station
programmes.description: Develop a crewed military reconnaissance station, optical instruments, secure downlinks, film-return procedures and its crew transport. Crewed intelligence has political visibility, finite endurance and high recurring cost.
programmes.historicalNote: Almaz military stations flew under the Salyut name. Salyut 2 failed in 1973; Salyut 3 flew in 1974 and Salyut 5 in 1976. Military station development is an alternative to civilian orbital science.

options.label: Bilateral docking demonstration
options.detail: Negotiate a joint mission, docking adapter and interoperable flight-control procedures with another space power.

options.label: International rescue standard
options.detail: Prioritise common docking interfaces and emergency procedures for later crew rescue. Certification needs flight evidence from compatible vehicles.

options.label: Joint science extension
options.detail: Study additional instruments and longer joint operations after the initial docking demonstration. More cooperation increases diplomatic and operational commitments.

options.label: Atmospheric balloon science

options.label: Halley encounter campaign

programmes.historicalNote: The Vega spacecraft launched in December 1984, delivered Venus landers and balloons in June 1985 and encountered Halley’s Comet in March 1986. This preview restricts launch to December 1984; missing this opportunity does not create another Halley encounter every 19 months. The trajectory and fifteen-month cruise remain schematic.

programmes.historicalNote: Apollo Applications was reduced to the Skylab programme. This entry preserves and expands the abandoned workshop campaign; it is a cancelled-plan continuation, distinct from historically flown Skylab.

outcomeDetails.full_success: Landing, rover deployment and the accepted mobile science campaign are confirmed. Mars mobile science is qualified.
outcomeDetails.partial_success: Useful landing or instrument data received, but rover deployment or the planned traverse is incomplete. Mobile science remains unqualified.
outcomeDetails.objective_failure: Landing, deployment or mobility failed; the principal rover objective was not achieved.
outcomeDetails.catastrophic_failure: The surface vehicle is lost. An extended technical investigation is required.

options.label: Direct return architecture

programmes.name: Mars Automated Ascent & Sample Return
programmes.description: Develop sterile sampling, a Mars ascent vehicle, orbital or direct return interfaces, an Earth-entry capsule and a secure sample-receiving facility. The mission lasts through sample recovery on Earth; surface collection alone earns no returned-sample capability.
programmes.historicalNote: NASA studied automated Mars sample return in 1970 and again in the mid-1970s. This is an unflown alternative programme, not a historical Cold War achievement. Its thirty-four-month campaign is a schematic round-trip duration.

outcomeDetails.full_success: The sample capsule is recovered on Earth and its containment is accepted. Mars sample return and robotic ascent-return are qualified.
outcomeDetails.partial_success: Useful surface, ascent or return data are recovered, but no accepted sample is delivered to the receiving laboratory. Sample return remains unqualified.
outcomeDetails.objective_failure: Sampling, ascent, return or Earth recovery failed. No returned-sample capability is awarded.
outcomeDetails.catastrophic_failure: The return system or sample is lost in a severe mission failure. Extended investigation and recovery review are required.

options.detail: Demonstrate maintenance, regenerative support and medical procedures over a twenty-four-month mission after hardware development.

options.label: Expedition shelter qualification
options.detail: Study radiation shelter geometry, consumables shielding and emergency procedures. Earth-orbit trials do not validate every deep-space radiation exposure.

options.label: Repair and reserve campaign
options.detail: Prioritise replaceable units, crew repair training, redundant support and a funded reserve of expedition hardware.

programmes.name: Expedition Habitat & Closed-Cycle Endurance Trials
programmes.description: Qualify expedition living volume, regenerative support, maintenance reserves, medical monitoring and storm-shelter procedures. A twenty-four-month orbital endurance campaign follows development; it tests habitation without claiming that Earth orbit reproduces the interplanetary radiation environment.
programmes.historicalNote: Long-duration habitats and planetary expeditions appeared in post-Apollo studies. This is a new alternative qualification programme, beyond the limited endurance inherited in 1970. Shielding and deep-space mission margins still require their own engineering.

outcomeDetails.full_success: The twenty-four-month orbital endurance trial is accepted. Expedition habitation is qualified within its demonstrated envelope.
outcomeDetails.partial_success: Useful endurance data are obtained, but the accepted two-year support and maintenance objectives remain incomplete.
outcomeDetails.objective_failure: A support-system deficiency forces termination of the endurance trial. Expedition habitation remains unqualified.
outcomeDetails.catastrophic_failure: A severe habitat emergency ends the trial. An extended crew-safety investigation is required.

options.label: Representative cargo demonstration
options.detail: Test expedition-scale descent and a representative landed mass before crew commitment.

options.label: Surface logistics package
options.detail: Study delivered power, habitat supplies and landing-site operations. Cargo delivery is not a crewed landing.

options.label: Conservative landing envelope
options.detail: Prioritise a restricted terrain envelope and measured terminal-descent margins rather than ambitious site access.

programmes.name: Mars Heavy Cargo Landing Demonstration
programmes.description: Qualify large aeroshell structures, guidance through a thin atmosphere, terminal propulsion, landing stability and cargo deployment. Deliver an uncrewed representative load before committing a crew. Small science-lander experience is insufficient for expedition-scale payloads.
programmes.historicalNote: Crewed Mars proposals required landers and surface logistics far beyond Viking-class payloads. This alternative demonstration is a new scale of engineering; no historic Cold War heavy Mars landing is implied.

outcomeDetails.full_success: The representative expedition-scale cargo is delivered and deployed on Mars. Heavy landing qualification is accepted.
outcomeDetails.partial_success: Useful descent or surface telemetry is recovered, but the representative cargo is not fully deployed. Heavy landing remains unqualified.
outcomeDetails.objective_failure: The heavy landing or cargo deployment failed. Further descent-system engineering is required.
outcomeDetails.catastrophic_failure: The heavy cargo vehicle is lost during arrival. An extended investigation is required.

options.label: Chemical propulsion expedition
options.detail: Retain a conventional propulsion route with a large launch and assembly campaign. Nuclear thermal propulsion is not a mandatory prerequisite.

options.label: Nuclear propulsion alternative
options.detail: Study a different transfer architecture only after separate reactor and flight qualification. This proposal confers no automatic risk or cost bonus.

options.label: Return-qualified surface expedition
options.detail: Qualify ascent, rendezvous, departure reserves and Earth recovery. A successful touchdown alone cannot satisfy the full expedition objective.

programmes.name: Crewed Mars Landing & Earth Return Expedition
programmes.description: Develop and qualify the complete expedition: orbital assembly, transfer propulsion, shielding, redundant support, surface habitat, ascent vehicle and Earth return. Include uncrewed ascent and return-hardware qualification before crew departure. The funded mission covers multiple launches, outbound flight, a surface expedition and the journey home. Full success is awarded only after crew recovery on Earth.
programmes.historicalNote: The 1969 Space Task Group considered crewed Mars missions during the 1980s. Those proposals did not become an operational programme. This entry is a high-cost counterfactual campaign; a chemical transfer architecture remains possible without mandatory nuclear propulsion. Thirty-four months represent a schematic conjunction-class round trip, not a precise trajectory.

outcomeDetails.full_success: The crew completes the Mars surface expedition and is recovered on Earth. Crewed Mars landing and return are jointly accepted.
outcomeDetails.partial_success: The crew returns after an abort or curtailed expedition, with useful flight data but without the complete accepted surface-and-return objective. The full landing-and-return capability remains unqualified.
outcomeDetails.objective_failure: The expedition aborts without completing an accepted surface mission. Major vehicle deficiencies require corrective engineering and a full technical review.
outcomeDetails.catastrophic_failure: Crew recovery fails after a catastrophic expedition emergency. An extended crew-safety investigation is required; the landing-and-return objective remains unfulfilled.

profiles.name: United States
profiles.startingSituation: The United States begins with operational crewed spaceflight, Saturn V and demonstrated lunar landing and return. New programmes retain their engineering, launch and operating costs.

profiles.name: Soviet Union
profiles.agency: National design bureaux and scientific space institutions
profiles.startingSituation: The Soviet Union begins with crewed orbital flight, automatic docking, lunar and planetary probe heritage. N1 heavy lift and a crewed lunar landing remain unfinished programmes.
inheritedInfrastructure: Crewed orbital spacecraft and mission control

profiles.name: France
profiles.startingSituation: France has independent orbital-launch experience from Diamant A. At the start of 1970 the Kourou Diamant B facilities are still being brought into service.

profiles.name: United Kingdom
profiles.agency: National space research and Black Arrow organisations
profiles.startingSituation: Britain has Ariel satellite and early Skynet operations, while Black Arrow has not yet achieved an orbital launch. British payload expertise and foreign launch access are separate from an independent launcher.
inheritedInfrastructure: Ariel scientific satellites and British-built Ariel 3

profiles.name: Japan
profiles.startingSituation: ISAS has substantial sounding-rocket and Lambda development experience. NASDA was established in 1969. No Japanese satellite has reached orbit on 1 January 1970; Ohsumi is still a pending mission.
inheritedInfrastructure: ISAS university research and launch teams
Kagoshima launch facilities and Lambda tests

profiles.name: China
profiles.agency: National defence and scientific space institutions
profiles.startingSituation: China has a major national launch and satellite development effort, but Dong Fang Hong 1 has not launched on 1 January 1970. Independent orbital access must still be demonstrated.
inheritedInfrastructure: Long March 1 development and ground tests

profiles.name: India
profiles.startingSituation: ISRO was established in August 1969 and inherits Thumba sounding-rocket work. India has no operational orbital satellite or qualified orbital launcher in January 1970.
strategicFocus: Satellite engineering and foreign launch access

profiles.name: Canada
profiles.startingSituation: Canada has Alouette heritage and the Canadian-built ISIS 1 mission launched by a US Delta in 1969. Payload design and operations are established; independent orbital launch production is not.
strategicFocus: Ground stations and purchased launch services

profiles.name: West Germany
profiles.agency: National research institutions and ESRO/ELDO partners
profiles.startingSituation: AZUR launched on a US Scout in November 1969. West Germany has satellite and ground-control experience through national and European cooperation, without an independent operational orbital launcher.

profiles.name: Italy
profiles.agency: San Marco programme and national research institutions
profiles.startingSituation: Italy operates the San Marco programme and equatorial ocean platforms. The programme uses US-provided Scout launch vehicles; the platform does not establish a domestic orbital rocket industry.

profiles.name: Australia
profiles.agency: National research, Woomera and tracking organisations
profiles.startingSituation: WRESAT reached orbit in 1967 using a donated US launcher. Australia has range, tracking and cooperation experience, but no independently produced orbital launch vehicle.

profiles.name: Netherlands
profiles.agency: National research organisations and ESRO partners
profiles.startingSituation: The Netherlands hosts ESTEC and has strong scientific instrument research. The ANS satellite is a study path in January 1970; formal national approval follows later in 1970.

profiles.name: Sweden
profiles.agency: National research institutions and ESRO partners
profiles.startingSituation: Esrange has operated under ESRO since 1966. Sweden has sounding-rocket, atmospheric and auroral science experience; the later Swedish space organisations are not treated as already founded in 1970.

profiles.name: Brazil
profiles.startingSituation: Brazil enters 1970 with CNAE, atmospheric research and Barreira do Inferno sounding-rocket infrastructure. Orbital satellites and independent orbital launch remain development objectives.

profiles.name: Argentina
profiles.startingSituation: Argentina has CNIE and a national sounding-rocket research tradition. Its 1970 starting point supports scientific payloads and launch-range work rather than a free orbital capability.

profiles.name: East Germany
profiles.agency: Academy of Sciences and Interkosmos Research Institutions
profiles.startingSituation: East Germany participates in Interkosmos and has already flown a photometer on Interkosmos 1 in October 1969. Its 1970 strengths are scientific instruments, optics, receiving stations and Soviet cooperation. Complete satellite manufacture, a domestic orbital launcher and national crew transport remain separate development objectives.
inheritedInfrastructure: Academy research and solar-terrestrial physics institutions
Neustrelitz ground reception and scientific data analysis

profiles.name: Player Country — New Space Programme
profiles.agency: To be established by the player
profiles.startingSituation: Any player-controlled country may begin here. Establish national coordination, then choose sounding research, spacecraft engineering, purchased foreign launch access or a gradual domestic launcher programme.
inheritedInfrastructure: No inherited satellites or orbital launcher
strategicFocus: Choose cooperation or an independent launch path

regions.name: Ground Infrastructure
regions.description: Launch ranges, tracking antennas, qualification laboratories and mission control. Ground assets are commissioned after development; they do not launch into orbit.

regions.name: Low Earth Orbit
regions.description: Crewed flight, orbital stations, astronomy and technology demonstrations. The close orbital environment still requires launch, power, communications and disposal planning.

regions.name: Polar & Sun-Synchronous Orbit
regions.description: Global imaging, reconnaissance and environmental monitoring. Inclination and local launch geography affect launch performance; this is a parallel mission architecture.

regions.name: Highly Elliptical Earth Orbit
regions.description: Molniya-type long dwell over high latitudes. Radiation exposure, repeated handovers and constellation replacement are continuing costs.

regions.name: Medium Earth Orbit
regions.description: Navigation and timing architectures between low orbit and the geostationary belt. A useful navigation service needs multiple spacecraft and a supported ground segment.

regions.name: Geostationary & Transfer Orbit
regions.description: Communications and fixed Earth coverage. Transfer-orbit injection, circularisation and station keeping consume performance and propellant.

regions.name: Cislunar Transfer & High Earth Orbit
regions.description: Translunar injection, high apogee tests and lunar-return trajectories. Transit flight, navigation and recovery are separate from a lunar landing.

regions.name: Lunar Orbit & Surface
regions.description: Orbital mapping, landing, rovers, sample return and crewed expeditions. Landing systems are required for surface work; direct lunar missions do not require Lagrange stations.

regions.name: Earth–Moon L1 / L2 Region
regions.description: The Earth–Moon pair of equilibrium regions, near the Moon. Relay or staging concepts need navigation and station keeping; this is distinct from Sun–Earth L1 and L2.

regions.name: Sun–Earth L1 Region
regions.description: Approximately 1.5 million km sunward from Earth. Solar-wind observatories use halo orbits and active station keeping; no lunar stop is necessary.

regions.name: Sun–Earth L2 Region
regions.description: Approximately 1.5 million km beyond Earth away from the Sun. Precision observatories require thermal control, communications and active station keeping.

regions.name: Venus & Inner-Planet Transfers
regions.description: Flybys, atmospheric entry and orbital radar science. Transfer opportunities and a severe thermal environment shape programme risk.

regions.name: Mercury Flyby Trajectories
regions.description: Inner-planet navigation and gravity-assist flybys. A Mercury flyby is an independent science branch; it is not a prerequisite for Mars.

regions.name: Mars Orbit, Surface & Return Missions
regions.description: Orbital reconnaissance, robotic landing, rovers, sample return and a counterfactual crewed expedition. Launch opportunities recur roughly every 26 months. Return missions include the complete outward cruise, surface campaign and journey home.

regions.name: Jupiter, Saturn & Outer Planets
regions.description: Multi-year cruises, radiation, weak communications and gravity-assist navigation. The map is schematic and does not represent relative distances.

milestones.title: First Artificial Satellite
milestones.summary: The first artificial satellite reaches Earth orbit.

milestones.title: First Human Spaceflight
milestones.summary: A human orbital mission is completed and its crew recovered.

milestones.title: First Crewed Lunar Landing
milestones.summary: A crew lands on the Moon and completes its accepted return mission.

milestones.title: First Successful Lunar Rover
milestones.summary: A robotic vehicle completes an accepted mobile science campaign on the Moon.

milestones.title: First Robotic Lunar Sample Return
milestones.summary: An automated mission delivers an accepted lunar sample to Earth.

milestones.title: First Operational Orbital Station
milestones.summary: A crewed orbital station completes its accepted initial scientific expedition.

milestones.title: First Successful Mars Orbiter
milestones.summary: A spacecraft enters Mars orbit and completes its accepted orbital science objectives.

milestones.title: First Sustained Mars Surface Mission
milestones.summary: A lander completes an accepted surface science campaign. Brief contact alone does not qualify.

milestones.title: First Successful Mars Rover
milestones.summary: A mobile explorer completes an accepted science traverse on Mars.

milestones.title: First Mars Samples Recovered on Earth
milestones.summary: A returned Mars sample is recovered and accepted by its receiving laboratory.

milestones.title: First Crewed Mars Expedition Returns
milestones.summary: The first accepted crewed Mars surface expedition returns its crew to Earth.
